titleEn: My God, my God, why have You forsaken me
progression: | Dm Dm | Gm Gm | Dm Am | Dm Dm |
intro: Thirty-two verses that begin at the bottom and end at the ends of the earth. Twenty-one verses of complaint, then one word in verse 22 that changes tense and everything with it, then ten verses of public praise that widen from one man to his brothers, to the assembly, to every family of the nations, to the dead. For a learner it is a drill in the object suffix: forsaken me, surrounded me, encircled me, closed in on me, answered me, save me. The same two letters at the end of verb after verb, first with enemies as the subject and then with God. A rabbinic tradition reads the superscription's hind of the dawn as Esther, and the psalm is associated with Purim.

stichs.en: For the leader; set to "The Hind of the Dawn."
A psalm of David.

verses.summary: A performance note, probably the name of a known melody. The image it leaves in the ear, first light after the longest part of the night, is the shape of the psalm that follows.

stichs.en: My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?
Far from my rescue are the words of my roaring.

verses.summary: The complaint is addressed, not thrown. The speaker still says my God twice before he says why, and the possessive is the whole argument of the psalm in one suffix.

stichs.en: My God, I call by day and You do not answer,
and by night, and there is no silence for me.

verses.summary: Day and night, and neither brings a reply. The last word is the point: it is not that God is silent, it is that the speaker cannot be.

stichs.en: And You are holy,
enthroned upon the praises of Israel.

verses.summary: The complaint does not become an accusation. God's holiness is conceded in the same breath as the abandonment, which is what makes the question hurt rather than dismiss.

stichs.en: In You our fathers trusted;
they trusted, and You delivered them.

verses.summary: The first of three verses that use the past as evidence. The verb for trust is repeated rather than varied, the way a person repeats a fact he is trying to make hold.

stichs.en: To You they cried out and they escaped;
in You they trusted and they were not ashamed.

verses.summary: Shame, not death, is named as the thing avoided. The fear running under the whole first half is that trusting publicly and getting nothing will make a fool of the one who trusted.

stichs.en: But I am a worm and not a man,
a reproach of humankind and despised by the people.

verses.summary: The pronoun is emphatic and set against the fathers of the previous verses. They were delivered; I am not even counted in the species.

stichs.en: All who see me mock me;
they part their lips, they shake the head.

verses.summary: Three verbs of face and gesture with no speech yet. The suffering is watched before it is commented on, which is the worse order.

stichs.en: "Roll it onto the LORD;
let Him rescue him, let Him deliver him,
since He delights in him."

verses.summary: The mockers quote the psalmist's own theology back at him. Every verb here is third person, which is the cruelty: they talk about him in front of him.

stichs.en: For You are the one who drew me from the womb,
who made me trust at my mother's breasts.

glosses: are the one who drew me out
verses.summary: The answer to the mockery is not a defence but an earlier date. Trust is described as something done to him before he could choose it.

stichs.en: Upon You I was cast from birth;
from my mother's belly You are my God.

verses.summary: The verb is the one used for throwing something away, turned into an image of being handed over. The word order at the end puts my God first and You are second, so the claim lands before the copula.

stichs.en: Do not be far from me,
for trouble is near,
for there is no one helping.

verses.summary: The first actual request in the psalm, ten verses in, and it asks for proximity rather than rescue. Far and near are placed against each other in consecutive clauses.

stichs.en: Many bulls have surrounded me;
the mighty ones of Bashan have encircled me.

verses.summary: The enemies become animals, and the grammar tightens with them: both lines end on a verb carrying the same object suffix, me. Bashan was cattle country east of the Jordan.

stichs.en: They open their mouth wide against me,
a lion tearing and roaring.

verses.summary: The lion enters the psalm here and will not leave until verse 22. Note that the psalmist's own roaring in verse 2 used a related noun; the sound he makes and the sound made at him are near neighbours.

stichs.en: Like water I am poured out,
and all my bones have come apart.
My heart has become like wax,
melting inside my innards.

verses.summary: The threat moves from outside to inside. Two similes of losing solid form, water and wax, describe a body that no longer holds its own shape.

stichs.en: My strength is dried up like a potsherd,
and my tongue sticks to my jaws,
and You lay me down in the dust of death.

verses.summary: After poured out and melted, dried out. The last verb is second person: the enemies did the surrounding, but the laying down in the dust is attributed to God.

stichs.en: For dogs have surrounded me,
a pack of evildoers has closed in on me,
like the lion, my hands and my feet.

glosses: they have closed in on me
verses.summary: The verse repeats the surrounding of verse 13 with dogs in place of bulls, and then breaks off into a clause with no verb in it. That missing verb is the most disputed word in the book; see the remez.

stichs.en: I can count all my bones;
they look on, they stare at me.

verses.summary: The verb for counting is the same root as the declaring in verse 23. Here he numbers his bones; there he will number God's acts to his brothers.

stichs.en: They divide my garments among themselves,
and for my clothing they cast lots.

verses.summary: The watchers become heirs. Dividing a living man's clothes assumes he is already dead, and the lot is what you cast when the thing cannot be split further.

stichs.en: But You, LORD, do not be far;
my strength, hurry to my help.

verses.summary: The plea of verse 12 returns, now with the divine name in it. The noun rendered my strength is rare and shares a root with the hind of the superscription.

stichs.en: Rescue my soul from the sword,
my only one from the paw of the dog.

verses.summary: My soul and my only one are parallel terms for the same thing, a life that has no spare. The dog of verse 17 comes back singular.

stichs.en: Save me from the lion's mouth,
and from the horns of wild oxen You have answered me.

verses.summary: The hinge of the psalm. The verse opens in the imperative and ends in the perfect: the request is still being made when the answer is reported as already given, and every verb after this one is praise.

stichs.en: I will declare Your name to my brothers;
in the midst of the assembly I will praise You.

verses.summary: The first audience of the rescue is other people. Deliverance in this psalm is not private; it is paid back by being told.

stichs.en: You who fear the LORD, praise Him;
all the seed of Jacob, honour Him,
and be in awe of Him, all the seed of Israel.

verses.summary: Three imperatives aimed outward. The speaker who could not get an answer is now the one giving instructions to a congregation.

stichs.en: For He did not despise and did not loathe
the affliction of the poor one,
and He did not hide His face from him,
and when he cried out to Him, He heard.

verses.summary: Four negations that answer the opening one by one. The question of verse 2 assumed abandonment; this verse denies it happened, without denying that it felt like it.

stichs.en: From You comes my praise in the great assembly;
my vows I will pay in front of those who fear Him.

verses.summary: Even the praise is sourced from God rather than produced by the speaker. Paying vows meant a thanksgiving offering, eaten in company, which is why the next verse has people at a meal.

stichs.en: The humble shall eat and be satisfied;
those who seek Him shall praise the LORD.
May your heart live forever.

verses.summary: The thanksgiving meal, and the poor are the ones fed by it. The last clause switches to direct address in the plural, a blessing spoken over the guests.

stichs.en: All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn back to the LORD,
and all the families of the nations shall bow down before You.

verses.summary: The circle widens past Israel. Remembering comes before turning back, which assumes the nations once knew and forgot rather than never knew at all.

stichs.en: For the kingship belongs to the LORD,
and He rules over the nations.

verses.summary: The reason the nations turn is stated as a fact about the present, not a prediction. Kingship is expressed with a preposition rather than a verb: it simply is His.

stichs.en: All the fat ones of the earth have eaten and bowed down;
before Him all who go down to the dust shall kneel,
even the one who could not keep his own soul alive.

verses.summary: The well fed and the dying are put at the same table. The dust here answers the dust of death in verse 16, and the last clause is difficult in Hebrew: translations differ over whether it describes the dying man or the speaker.

stichs.en: A seed shall serve Him;
it shall be told of the Lord to the coming generation.

verses.summary: The word for seed was used twice in verse 24 for Jacob and Israel and returns here without a name attached, so the line reaches forward rather than back.

stichs.en: They shall come and tell His righteousness
to a people yet to be born, that He has done it.

verses.summary: The psalm ends on a bare verb with no object: He has done it. What began as a private question closes as a report handed to people who do not exist yet.

pardes.body: Two unequal halves joined by one word. Verses 2 to 21 are complaint: abandonment, mockery, bulls, dogs, a body coming apart, clothes already divided. Verses 23 to 32 are praise, and it expands in stages, from brothers to assembly to the seed of Jacob to every family of the nations to those going down to the dust. The join is {{22.5}}, a perfect tense meaning You have answered me, sitting at the end of a verse that began by begging to be saved. Nothing in the text narrates the rescue. It is simply spoken of as done, and everything after it is in a different key. Read straight through, the psalm is one person's account of what it is like to be answered late.

{{17.6}} is one of the most disputed words in the Hebrew Bible, and the honest report is that it is not settled. The Masoretic Text, the received Jewish text, vocalizes it as a preposition plus the noun for lion, giving "like the lion, my hands and my feet." That clause has no verb, which is unusual but not impossible in poetry; traditional Jewish commentary supplies the sense from the image already running through verses 14 and 22, a lion's mouth on the hands and feet. Some Hebrew manuscripts, and a Psalms scroll found at Nahal Hever, read a form ending in a different final letter, which has been taken as a verb and translated "they dug" or "they bound" or "they pierced"; the ancient Greek version reads a verb of digging, and Christian tradition has read it as piercing. The two readings differ by one letter, and the two letters concerned are close enough in the square script that scribes confuse them elsewhere. This page does not decide between them. It notes that the Masoretic reading is the text Jewish liturgy and commentary work from, that the variant is real and old, and that the verse is hard in every version. Elsewhere in the psalm the wordplay is easier to see: the roaring of {{2.7}} and the roaring lion of verse 14 are near neighbours, and the rare noun for strength in {{20.4}} shares a root with the hind of {{1.2}}.

A rabbinic tradition reads the hind of the dawn in {{1.2}} and {{1.3}} as Esther, and the psalm has been attached to Purim on that basis: the dawn that arrives only after the night has gone as far as it can, and a deliverance that appears with no visible miracle in it. Read that way the speaker is not only David but the community in exile, and the mockers of verse 9 who say let God rescue him are the taunt of every generation that watched Jews trust and get nothing. The reading also explains why the second half insists so hard on public telling: an act of rescue that leaves no trace has to be declared or it is lost. The verse that answers the opening is {{25.8}} and {{25.9}}, He did not hide His face. The Torah's own phrase for exile is the hiding of the face, and the psalm ends by denying that the hiding was ever an abandonment, without pretending it was not felt as one.

In the mystical reading the superscription is the whole map. First light is measured from the darkest point, and the psalm insists that the two are the same event seen from different ends of the night. The moment of maximum concealment, {{2.3}}, and the declaration that no face was ever hidden, {{25.8}}, are one state described twice. The kabbalistic tradition reads the hiding of the face as contraction rather than absence, a withdrawal that makes room for a creature to exist as a separate self and therefore to cry out at all. On that reading the unanswered calling of verse 3 is not a failure of the relation but its cost, and the last three words of the psalm, He has done it, are put in the perfect because from the far side the whole night reads as a single completed act.
